text:
[
  {
    "n": 1,
    "title": "Conditional Probability and the Reduced Sample Space",
    "scope": "Establishes the formal definition of conditional probability as a measure on a contracted sample space. Explains why the conditioning event acts as the new universe of outcomes and why the denominator normalizes the remaining probability mass. Covers the distinction between conditioning orders and directional conditioning with concrete empirical and theoretical examples.",
    "key_points": [
      "Definition: $P(B|A) = \\frac{P(A \\cap B)}{P(A)}$, strictly defined only when $P(A) > 0$",
      "Concept of reduced sample space: conditioning on $A$ eliminates outcomes outside $A$, restricting $S$ to $A$ and scaling probabilities by $\\frac{1}{P(A)}$",
      "Directional asymmetry: $P(B|A) \\neq P(A|B)$ in general because the reference conditioning events differ",
      "Empirical demonstration with flight delays: $P(D) = 0.83$, $P(A) = 0.82$, $P(D \\cap A) = 0.78$, yielding $P(A|D) = \\frac{0.78}{0.83} \\approx 0.94$ versus $P(D|A) = \\frac{0.78}{0.82} \\approx 0.95$",
      "Loaded die demonstration: odd outcomes have weight $w = 1/9$, even outcomes have $2w = 2/9$; evaluating perfect square $B = \\{1, 4\\}$ given $A = \\{4, 5, 6\\}$ yields $P(B|A) = \\frac{2/9}{5/9} = \\frac{2}{5} \\neq P(B) = \\frac{1}{3}$, proving probabilistic dependence"
    ]
  },
  {
    "n": 2,
    "title": "Independence of Two Events",
    "scope": "Defines statistical independence between two events and differentiates it from mutual exclusivity. Shows that independence means knowledge of one event provides zero predictive information about the other. Demonstrates that events originating from a single trial can still be mutually independent.",
    "key_points": [
      "Definition: $A$ and $B$ are independent iff $P(B|A) = P(B)$ or $P(A|B) = P(A)$ (assuming conditional probabilities exist); otherwise they are dependent",
      "Equivalent product formulation: $A$ and $B$ are independent iff $P(A \\cap B) = P(A)P(B)$",
      "Critical distinction between independence ($P(A \\cap B) = P(A)P(B)$) and mutual exclusivity ($A \\cap B = \\emptyset$ so $P(A \\cap B) = 0$)",
      "Fair die demonstration: $A = \\{2, 4, 6\\}$ (even, $P(A) = 1/2$) and $B = \\{3, 6\\}$ (multiple of 3, $P(B) = 1/3$), where $A \\cap B = \\{6\\}$ has $P(A \\cap B) = 1/6$; evaluating $P(A|B) = \\frac{1/6}{1/3} = 1/2 = P(A)$ proves independence within the exact same physical roll"
    ]
  },
  {
    "n": 3,
    "title": "The Multiplication Rule for Two Events",
    "scope": "Formulates the general multiplication (product) rule for computing intersection probabilities. Covers sampling without replacement and contrasts dependent sequential events with independent parallel systems. Teaches how to translate sequential physical processes into formal intersections.",
    "key_points": [
      "Theorem: $P(A \\cap B) = P(A)P(B|A) = P(B)P(A|B)$, provided conditioning events have non-zero probability",
      "Specialization for independent events: $P(A \\cap B) = P(A)P(B)$",
      "Dependent sampling without replacement: drawing 2 defectives from 20 fuses (5 defective) yields $P(A \\cap B) = P(A)P(B|A) = \\left(\\frac{5}{20}\\right)\\left(\\frac{4}{19}\\right) = \\frac{1}{19}$",
      "Independent system reliability: emergency services where fire engine availability is $P(A) = 0.98$ and ambulance availability is $P(B) = 0.92$, giving joint availability $P(A \\cap B) = (0.98)(0.92) = 0.9016$"
    ]
  },
  {
    "n": 4,
    "title": "General Chain Rule and Mutual Independence of Multiple Events",
    "scope": "Extends the multiplication rule to an arbitrary collection of $k$ events via the probability chain rule. Defines mutual independence across $n$ events and explains why product factorization of the total intersection is insufficient. Uses counterexamples and sequential card sampling without replacement.",
    "key_points": [
      "General Chain Rule: $P(A_1 \\cap A_2 \\cap \\dots \\cap A_k) = P(A_1)P(A_2|A_1)P(A_3|A_1 \\cap A_2) \\dots P(A_k|A_1 \\cap \\dots \\cap A_{k-1})$",
      "Chain rule application: drawing 3 cards without replacement (first is red ace, second is 10 or jack, third is strictly between 3 and 7) yields $P(A_1 \\cap A_2 \\cap A_3) = \\left(\\frac{2}{52}\\right)\\left(\\frac{8}{51}\\right)\\left(\\frac{12}{50}\\right) = \\frac{8}{5525}$",
      "Definition of mutual independence: a collection $\\mathcal{A} = \\{A_1, \\dots, A_n\\}$ is mutually independent iff for every subset $\\{A_{i_1}, \\dots, A_{i_k}\\}$ ($k \\le n$), $P(A_{i_1} \\cap \\dots \\cap A_{i_k}) = \\prod_{j=1}^k P(A_{i_j})$",
      "Insufficiency of whole-set factorization: counterexample where $A = B$ and $C = \\emptyset$, giving $P(A \\cap B \\cap C) = 0 = P(A)P(B)P(C)$ even though identical non-trivial events $A$ and $B$ are completely dependent"
    ]
  },
  {
    "n": 5,
    "title": "The Law of Total Probability",
    "scope": "Presents partitions of sample spaces and derives the Law of Total Probability. Proves rigorously that any event can be decomposed into disjoint intersections across a partition. Applies the theorem to two-stage transfer experiments without replacement.",
    "key_points": [
      "Definition of partition: events $B_1, \\dots, B_k$ are pairwise mutually exclusive ($B_i \\cap B_j = \\emptyset$) and exhaustive ($\\bigcup_{i=1}^k B_i = S$) with $P(B_i) > 0$",
      "Decomposition identity: $A = (B_1 \\cap A) \\cup (B_2 \\cap A) \\cup \\dots \\cup (B_k \\cap A)$ where all terms are pairwise disjoint",
      "Theorem & Proof: $P(A) = \\sum_{i=1}^k P(B_i \\cap A) = \\sum_{i=1}^k P(B_i)P(A|B_i)$ using finite additivity of probability measures and the product rule",
      "Two-stage transfer problem: Bag 1 (4W, 3B), Bag 2 (3W, 5B); transfer 1 ball unseen from Bag 1 to Bag 2, then draw from Bag 2: $P(B_2) = P(B_1)P(B_2|B_1) + P(W_1)P(B_2|W_1) = \\left(\\frac{3}{7}\\right)\\left(\\frac{6}{9}\\right) + \\left(\\frac{4}{7}\\right)\\left(\\frac{5}{9}\\right) = \\frac{38}{63}$"
    ]
  },
  {
    "n": 6,
    "title": "Bayes' Rule and Posterior Inference",
    "scope": "Formulates and proves Bayes' Rule for inverting conditional probabilities over a partitioned sample space. Explains how prior probabilities are updated into posterior probabilities upon observing evidence. Connects the numerator to the joint product rule and the denominator to the Law of Total Probability.",
    "key_points": [
      "Bayes' Rule Theorem: $P(B_r|A) = \\frac{P(B_r \\cap A)}{\\sum_{i=1}^k P(B_i \\cap A)} = \\frac{P(B_r)P(A|B_r)}{\\sum_{i=1}^k P(B_i)P(A|B_i)}$ for any partition element $B_r$ and event $A$ with $P(A) > 0$",
      "Formal proof: substitution of $P(B_r \\cap A) = P(B_r)P(A|B_r)$ into the definition $P(B_r|A) = \\frac{P(B_r \\cap A)}{P(A)}$ alongside the Law of Total Probability expansion of $P(A)$",
      "Conceptual mechanism: updating prior probability $P(B_r)$ to posterior probability $P(B_r|A)$ via the likelihood factor $P(A|B_r)$ normalized by the marginal evidence $P(A)$"
    ]
  },
  {
    "n": 7,
    "title": "Random Variables and Sample Space Classification",
    "scope": "Introduces the formal mathematical definition of a random variable as a real-valued mapping from a sample space. Differentiates discrete from continuous sample spaces and sets up the event-theoretic meaning of numerical assignments. Covers standard structural examples including counts of defectives and indicator functions.",
    "key_points": [
      "Definition: a random variable $X$ is a function $X: S \\to \\mathbb{R}$ that assigns a real number $x$ to each outcome in the sample space $S$",
      "Notation: capital letter $X$ denotes the random variable (the function); lowercase $x$ denotes a specific realized value",
      "Pre-image as an event: the expression $\\{X = x\\}$ represents the subset event $\\{\\omega \\in S : X(\\omega) = x\\}$ (e.g., testing 3 electronic components where $S = \\{NNN, \\dots, DDD\\}$ gives $\\{X = 2\\} = \\{DDN, DND, NDD\\}$)",
      "Urn extraction mapping: drawing 2 balls without replacement from 4 red and 3 black gives $Y \\in \\{0, 1, 2\\}$ corresponding to subsets $\\{BB\\}$, $\\{RB, BR\\}$, and $\\{RR\\}$",
      "Bernoulli/Indicator variable: $X = 1$ if an item is defective, $0$ if nondefective",
      "Sample space classification: discrete (finite or countably infinite elements matching whole numbers) versus continuous (uncountably infinite elements matching a continuum/interval, e.g., particle decay time $S = [0, \\infty) \\subset \\mathbb{R}$)"
    ]
  },
  {
    "n": 8,
    "title": "Probability Mass Functions (PMF) and Hypergeometric Modeling",
    "scope": "Defines the probability mass function (PMF) for discrete random variables and specifies its axiomatic properties. Demonstrates the construction of distribution tables from coin tosses. Derives and applies the hypergeometric distribution formula for finite population sampling without replacement.",
    "key_points": [
      "Definition of PMF: the function $f(x) = P(X = x)$ characterizing the discrete random variable $X$",
      "Axiomatic properties: (1) $f(x) \\ge 0$, (2) $\\sum_x f(x) = 1$, (3) $P(X = x) = f(x)$",
      "Coin-toss distribution construction: 3 coin tosses with $M = \\text{number of heads}$ yields $f(0) = 1/8$, $f(1) = 3/8$, $f(2) = 3/8$, $f(3) = 1/8$",
      "Combinations review: $\\binom{n}{r} = \\frac{n!}{r!(n - r)!}$",
      "Hypergeometric formula: $P(X = x) = \\frac{\\binom{K}{x}\\binom{N - K}{n - x}}{\\binom{N}{n}}$ for population size $N$, defectives $K$, and sample size $n$",
      "Laptop purchase calculation ($N = 20, K = 3, n = 2$): $f(0) = \\frac{\\binom{3}{0}\\binom{17}{2}}{\\binom{20}{2}} = \\frac{68}{95}$, $f(1) = \\frac{\\binom{3}{1}\\binom{17}{1}}{\\binom{20}{2}} = \\frac{51}{190}$, $f(2) = \\frac{\\binom{3}{2}\\binom{17}{0}}{\\binom{20}{2}} = \\frac{3}{190}$, with sum verification $\\frac{136 + 51 + 3}{190} = 1$"
    ]
  },
  {
    "n": 9,
    "title": "Cumulative Distribution Functions (CDF) for Discrete Random Variables",
    "scope": "Defines the cumulative distribution function (CDF) for discrete random variables as an accumulation of probability mass. Explains the step-function structure, domain, and right-continuity. Derives the closed-form piecewise CDF from the laptop sampling PMF.",
    "key_points": [
      "Definition: $F(x) = P(X \\le x) = \\sum_{t \\le x} f(t)$ defined for all real numbers $-\\infty < x < \\infty$",
      "Structural nature: step function with jump discontinuities at support points $x$ where jump height equals $f(x)$, constant between support points, right-continuous everywhere",
      "Piecewise construction for laptop distribution: $F(x) = 0$ for $x < 0$; $F(x) = \\frac{136}{190}$ for $0 \\le x < 1$; $F(x) = \\frac{187}{190}$ for $1 \\le x < 2$; $F(x) = 1$ for $x \\ge 2$"
    ]
  }
]
